topic: Should nuclear energy capacity be expanded rapidly?

turns.content: I support expanding nuclear energy, although I must admit the economics look difficult at first glance. The upfront picture is intimidating: nuclear power is prohibitively expensive and economically unviable for most utilities, with new plants costing many billions and taking a decade to complete. Private investors therefore hesitate, and I believe only a tiny pilot program of one or two small reactors makes sense until costs fall dramatically. The technology itself is proven and safe, and waste volumes are small compared with the energy produced, so the long-term promise remains attractive. Still, my position is that rapid expansion would be financially reckless right now, and governments should limit themselves to research funding plus a single demonstration site. A cautious, minimal approach respects both the climate need and the harsh budget reality that currently constrains every utility planning department.

Rapid nuclear expansion is the wrong priority because cheaper, faster options already exist. Wind and solar farms can be permitted and connected in two to three years at a fraction of nuclear capital costs, and grid-scale batteries now cover evening peaks that critics once claimed required baseload plants. Every billion committed to a reactor that delivers power in fifteen years is a billion diverted from efficiency retrofits and transmission upgrades that cut emissions this decade. Uranium supply chains concentrate in a handful of countries, recreating the geopolitical dependencies we are trying to escape, while waste repositories remain politically stalled after decades of effort. Communities near proposed sites consistently organize against them, adding years of litigation. A climate strategy must spend limited funds where each dollar displaces the most carbon the fastest, and that test points away from rapid nuclear construction.

My opponent recites outdated cost figures that ignore the revolution in reactor economics. Modern standardized designs have flipped the equation entirely: nuclear is the cheapest option available per megawatt-hour once factories produce identical modules at scale, far below wind, solar, and especially batteries. Because the fuel is so cheap, we should authorize hundreds of reactors immediately and blanket every region with abundant near-free electricity, since costs will keep falling the more we build. The budget concerns I raised earlier no longer apply, because new financing models and factory assembly have eliminated the overruns of the past. Waste fears are equally obsolete, as recycling consumes nearly all spent fuel. Any delay now is pure sabotage of the climate, and utilities that refuse to order reactors this year should face penalties for obstructing the cheapest option available to humanity.

My opponent has just demolished his own case, and the judges should notice. In his opening he insisted nuclear power is prohibitively expensive and only a tiny pilot makes sense, yet now he claims it is the cheapest option available and demands hundreds of reactors immediately. Both statements cannot be true, and a debater who reverses his core economic premise mid-round cannot be trusted on any figure he cites. Beyond the contradiction, his rebuttal offers no evidence for the alleged factory revolution, no named design, no cost study, and no explanation of how financing risks vanished in a single speech. My case, by contrast, has remained consistent: deployment speed, capital cost, waste politics, and community consent all favor renewables and grid investment. A side that contradicts its own foundation has conceded the round.
